title: Follow Caleb from the scouting trip to Hebron

hebron.name: Hebron
hebron.text: Ancient Hebron is identified with Tel Rumeida, beside the modern city of Hebron (al-Khalil). It is one of the highest towns in the hill country of Judah. Long before Caleb, Abraham camped at the great trees of Mamre nearby, and the patriarchs were buried in the cave of Machpelah here (Genesis 13:18; 23:19; 49:29–31).

eshcol.name: Valley of Eshcol
eshcol.text: Numbers 13:23–24 places Eshcol near Hebron. The spies cut a single cluster of grapes so heavy that two of them carried it on a pole. Tradition points to the fertile valleys just north of Hebron, which are still known for vineyards.

kadesh.name: Kadesh Barnea
kadesh.text: The spies left from, and returned to, Kadesh in the wilderness (Numbers 13:26; Joshua 14:7). Numbers links it to both the Desert of Paran and the Desert of Zin. Most scholars identify it with the spring and oasis at Ein el-Qudeirat in the northeastern Sinai.

gilgal.name: Gilgal
gilgal.text: Israel’s first camp west of the Jordan, “on the eastern border of Jericho” (Joshua 4:19). Here the men of Judah came to Joshua and Caleb made his request (Joshua 14:6). Several sites near Jericho have been proposed, but none is confirmed.

debir.name: Debir
debir.text: Caleb promised his daughter Achsah in marriage to the man who captured Kiriath Sepher, later called Debir. His nephew Othniel took it (Joshua 15:15–17). Khirbet Rabud, southwest of Hebron, is widely favored; Tell Beit Mirsim is an older proposal.

beersheba.name: Beersheba
beersheba.text: Tel Beersheba marks the heart of the northern Negev, the dry country the spies crossed as they went up through the Negev to Hebron (Numbers 13:22). The text does not say they stopped here.

jerusalem.name: Jerusalem
jerusalem.text: Shown for orientation. In Caleb’s day this was the Jebusite city of Jebus, and Judah could not drive the Jebusites out (Joshua 15:8, 63).

chapters.title: Sent out from Kadesh
chapters.html:
Moses chose one leader from each tribe to explore Canaan. For Judah he chose Caleb son of Jephunneh (Numbers 13:6). Caleb later said he was forty years old at the time (Joshua 14:7).

Their orders were to go up through the Negev into the hill country and see whether the people were strong or weak, the towns walled or open, and the soil rich or poor. The survey took forty days and reached as far north as Rehob, near Lebo Hamath, well off this map.
quote: Go up through the Negev and on into the hill country.
facts: From Kadesh to Hebron is about 73 miles (118 km) in a straight line, and the land climbs about 1,600 feet (500 m) on the way.
Ein el-Qudeirat, the favored site of Kadesh, has one of the strongest springs in the northern Sinai, which explains why a large camp could stay there.

chapters.title: Hebron and the sons of Anak
chapters.html:
Hebron is the only town the spy account names along the way. There they saw Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai, descendants of Anak. The text notes that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt, so it was already an old city (Numbers 13:22).

Nearby, in the Valley of Eshcol, they cut a cluster of grapes so large that two men carried it on a pole. Remember those three names. They come back at the end of the story.
facts: Eshcol means “cluster,” and the Hebron hills are still famous for grapes today.
The two spies carrying grapes on a pole became the logo of Israel’s Ministry of Tourism.

chapters.title: Two reports at Kadesh
chapters.html:
Back at Kadesh, all the scouts agreed the land flowed with milk and honey. Ten of them said its cities were fortified and its people so large that “we seemed like grasshoppers” (Numbers 13:33).

Caleb quieted the crowd and urged Israel to go up at once. God said his servant Caleb had a different spirit and followed him wholeheartedly (Numbers 14:24). The rest of that generation would die in the wilderness during forty years of wandering.
quote: We should go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly do it.
facts: Of the twelve scouts, only Caleb and Joshua lived to enter the land (Numbers 14:30, 38).

chapters.title: Forty-five years later, at Gilgal
chapters.html:
After the wilderness years and the first campaigns in Canaan, the men of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. Caleb reminded him of Moses’ promise that the land his feet had walked on would belong to him and his descendants (Deuteronomy 1:36).

At eighty-five he said he was as strong as the day Moses sent him. He did not ask for easy ground. He asked for the high, fortified hill country where the Anakites still lived.
quote: Now give me this hill country that the LORD promised me that day.
facts: The Jordan Valley near Jericho lies about 800 feet below sea level. Hebron stands above 3,000 feet, so Caleb was asking for a climb of nearly 4,000 feet.

chapters.title: Hebron becomes Caleb’s
chapters.html:
Joshua blessed Caleb and gave him Hebron, earlier called Kiriath Arba after Arba, the greatest of the Anakites. Caleb drove out Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai (Joshua 15:14), the same three names the spies had reported forty-five years before.

Later, Hebron itself became a Levitical city of refuge, and Caleb kept its fields and villages (Joshua 20:7; 21:11–12).
facts: Hebron later became David’s first capital. He reigned there for seven and a half years before moving to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:5).

chapters.title: Debir, Othniel and Achsah
chapters.html:
From Hebron, Caleb moved against Debir, earlier called Kiriath Sepher. He promised his daughter Achsah to whoever captured it. Othniel, son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz, took the town and later became Israel’s first judge (Judges 3:9–11).

Achsah asked her father for more than dry Negev land, and Caleb gave her the upper and lower springs (Joshua 15:19). In this hill country, water decided whether an inheritance could be lived on.
facts: Kiriath Sepher means “town of the book” or “town of scribes.”
